newsitem.title: USA: U.S. copper market eyes COMEX stocks in Baltimore.
newsitem.headline: U.S. copper market eyes COMEX stocks in Baltimore.

text.p: As talk continues of hidden stocks of copper in Europe and China, traders in the U.S. are watching carefully the fate of their own new and very visible stockpile in COMEX's Baltimore warehouse.
On Tuesday 620 short tons of copper entered Baltimore, followed by another 526 short tons on Wednesday.
The talk is that 8,000 to 10,000 tons had been on board the vessel that docked at Baltimore, with 2,000 tons already sold to consumers.

There have been rumours for some time that copper from LME warehouses in Europe, especially Hamburg, was wending its way to the U.S. on the back of lucrative arbitrage deals between the London and New York exchanges.
"I think this would help explain where some of the copper from Europe went," a producer-linked trader said. "But I would expect it to come out between now and the end of January."
COMEX stocks total 32,374 short tons as of Wednesday.

Traders said COMEX inventory in Baltimore, Tucson and San Manuel - totalling 28,836 short tons - have risen largely because of arbitrage deals when the COMEX premium over LME ballooned to some four cents per pound.
Much of the metal going into Tuscson and San Manuel was from the LME warehouse in Long Beach, traders have said.
But several traders have suggested there is an added twist to the Baltimore cross-exchange shuffle - a desire to rein in the arbitrage.
"If it's going into COMEX then I guess they are trying to bring in the arb," a merchant said.
A trader added, "I would think its influence is gradually showing its impact right now."
COMEX November to LME November premium was shrinking to about 1.75 cents, down from 3.0 to 4.0 cents previously, the trader noted.
Some questioned the economics of the strategy to influence the arb. "It made no sense. No matter when they put the arbitrage on, to bring it here and put it on warrant, it's a loser," a dealer said.

"Whoever did it could not justify it and say they were making a profit. The shipper has not, until very recently, offered it to consumers, so their intent all along was to influence the market," the dealer added.
Placing the metal on warrant in Baltimore instead of selling it to U.S. consumers, the shipper missed out on a 2 to 3 cent per pound profit, some traders estimated.

COMEX premiums over LME soared when COMEX stocks tumbled to below 20,000 tons. Those who held the remaining stocks declined to lend them into the market, and took an equal or greater spread position, a trader suggested. That position was sold later at a profit once the spread widened.
But some thought material in Baltimore was unlikely to fester because of good demand for cathode on the U.S. East Coast where many rod mills are located.

"I don't see it staying long in the warehouse and any hope of influencing the arbitrage will be washed away," the merchant said. "I don't think material can sit on the East Coast, that's why it's never been there before."
Another trader added, "If we took delivery of the Baltimore warrants as a merchant, it would be out as fast as we could sell it."
-- New York Commodities 212-859-1646
